extracted.intended_audience: university mathematicians, mathematics education researchers, and instructors interested in how mathematicians and teachers make sense of and teach definitions
extracted.subtask_description: Study of the processes and instructional moves mathematicians use to understand, evaluate, and teach new mathematical definitions, based on interviews and a definition task. Emphasizes examples, decoding notation, contextualizing purpose, and pedagogical moves for supporting student understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features valued by mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should be unambiguous, logically equivalent to other definitions of the same concept, hierarchical, stated in a usable form, and should address the purpose for which they were invented (Harel, Selden, & Selden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when judging a definition: check for ambiguity, equivalence to alternative formulations, place in a hierarchy of concepts, practical usability (can it be applied?), and whether it serves the intended mathematical purpose. If one of these is lacking, the definition may need revision or further justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples to test and internalize definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I immediately try to think of examples of what would satisfy the requirements of the definition and what not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering a definition, generate 'standard examples' (e.g., real line, integers under addition) to test whether they satisfy the definition. Use examples to identify essential features captured by the definition and to check for unexpected inclusions or exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-examples (counter-examples) to delineate boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions exclude things; a definition should tell you not only what is in the class but what is not. Provide examples where the definition does not apply and identify which part of the definition fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present non-examples alongside positive examples to clarify the boundaries of the definition. Ask 'what part of the definition goes wrong here?' to focus student attention on essential conditions. Non-examples are key for preventing overgeneralized concept images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriately-scaled examples
rubrics_metrics.description: "Choose the right example, not too trivial but not too complicated, in order to focus attention on the essential features."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select examples that are informative: avoid trivial cases that hide structure and avoid overly complex examples that distract from the central idea. For teaching, present a progression of examples that gradually reveal crucial aspects of the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams or visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming the definition into something more visual (draw pictures/diagrams) helps to work out the essential features, even for algebraic or abstract definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, create visual representations or sketches to make abstract relationships concrete. Use visuals to test hypotheses about the definition and to communicate structure to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parse and decode phrasing and notation (decoding process)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The phrasing has to get parsed; torn apart." Pay attention to words, notation, and quantifiers and engage in a decoding process to understand component parts of the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully analyze each phrase, symbol, and quantifier in the statement. Request or provide supporting definitions of related terms. Misreading notation or quantifiers often causes misunderstanding—treat decoding as the first step before example-generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide and consult supporting definitions and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding often requires supporting definitions (e.g., support, formal power series) and worked examples; these should be available and consulted as part of sense-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing a definition, supply definitions of related terms and at least one explicit example. In interviews/tasks, offer supporting materials on request. For instruction, make related terminology and examples explicit and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the definition to familiar terms, contexts, and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: See the definition 'in context' and connect it to other words or concepts already known; show how the notion is used in practice or in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link new definitions to students' prior knowledge and to familiar mathematical settings. Provide references or instances where the definition is used to prove results; demonstrating usefulness helps students (and mathematicians) internalize the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the definition's usefulness for intended mathematical work
rubrics_metrics.description: "Is this some notion that will actually be useful to prove the kind of results you are interested in?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the definition captures features needed for theorems or constructions of interest. If a definition is too general or too narrow relative to intended applications, reconsider its formulation or motivate the generality with examples of its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a varied collection of examples to explore essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine a range of examples (including ones built from simple examples and ones that differ) to identify necessary conditions and what the definition intends to 'capture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on a single example. Build families of examples and search for ones that reveal different facets of the definition. Use this process to refine understanding and to test whether the definition omits important cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, iterative engagement and consulting literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing understanding of a definition requires purposeful engagement over time, including consulting texts and other sources for examples and clarifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sense-making as iterative: read, parse, test with examples, consult references, and revisit the definition. Document where further information or usage examples are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical moves to support student-centered understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher moves identified include 'zooming out, illustrative real world examples, counter-examples, selective restating, appealing to definitions, and intentional sequencing of student sharing.' These moves can help open a class to student-focused instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these moves to guide inquiry-oriented lessons: zoom out to provide perspective, introduce vivid or real-world examples to motivate, present counter-examples to clarify boundaries, selectively restate student contributions to highlight mathematical points, and explicitly appeal to definitions when productive. Design professional development to shift responsibility for restating and introducing examples to students over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional sequencing of student sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize student contributions into a logical order (e.g., call on less-mature groups first and more formal/complete groups later) to guide the flow and trajectory of classroom discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facilitating group presentations, evaluate group readiness and choose sequence strategically to build ideas progressively; watch for incomplete knowledge (e.g., unknown status of a group's definition) and adjust sequencing if necessary. Use the final, most formal group as a launching point for whole-class discussion.
